title: test-0021-SCI-PHY-MEASURE
passage: Measuring distances accurately requires standard tools and proper techniques. Long ago, people used handspans or footsteps, but these vary from person to person, making them unreliable for consistent results. Today, we use standard units like the metre, which is defined globally. When using a ruler, you must place your eye directly above the mark to avoid parallax errors; looking from the side leads to incorrect readings. If your ruler has a broken zero end, you can simply start measuring from any other clear mark, like 1 cm, and subtract that value from your final reading. Measuring curved lines is also possible by using a piece of thread to trace the path and then measuring the thread against a straight scale. Furthermore, motion takes many forms. A pendulum swings back and forth in a periodic motion, while a spinning top rotates in circular motion. Some objects, like a moving bicycle, exhibit complex motion by combining rotation with forward travel. Importantly, motion is simply a change in an object's position over time, regardless of whether it moves toward you or away from you. Understanding these principles ensures that our measurements are precise and our descriptions of movement are scientifically accurate.
